# cfg_aliases - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg_aliases/^0.2.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cfg-aliases)CFG Aliases

CFG Aliases is a tiny utility to help save you a lot of effort with long winded `#[cfg()]` checks. This crate provides a single [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro that doesn’t have any dependencies and specifically avoids pulling in

`syn` or `quote` so that the impact on your comile times should be negligible.You use the the [ cfg_aliases!](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html) macro in your

`build.rs` script to define aliases such as `x11` that could then be used in the `cfg` attribute or macro for conditional compilation: `#[cfg(x11)]`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[build-dependencies]
cfg_aliases = "0.1.0"
```
**build.rs:**

```
use cfg_aliases::cfg_aliases;
fn main() {
    // Setup cfg aliases
    cfg_aliases! {
        // Platforms
        wasm: { target_arch = "wasm32" },
        android: { target_os = "android" },
        macos: { target_os = "macos" },
        linux: { target_os = "linux" },
        // Backends
        surfman: { all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(wasm)) },
        glutin: { all(feature = "glutin", not(wasm)) },
        wgl: { all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(wasm)) },
        dummy: { not(any(wasm, glutin, wgl, surfman)) },
    }
}
```
Now that we have our aliases setup we can use them just like you would expect:

```
#[cfg(wasm)]
println!("This is running in WASM");
#[cfg(surfman)]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(dummy)]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
This greatly improves what would otherwise look like this without the aliases:

```
#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
println!("We're running in WASM");
#[cfg(all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "22")))]
{
    // Do stuff related to surfman
}
#[cfg(not(any(
    target_arch = "wasm32",
    all(unix, feature = "surfman", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(windows, feature = "wgl", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
    all(feature = "glutin", not(target_arch = "wasm32")),
)))]
println!("We're in dummy mode, specify another feature if you want a smarter app!");
```
You can also use the `cfg!` macro or combine your aliases with other checks using `all()`, `not()`, and `any()`. Your aliases are genuine `cfg` flags now!

```
if cfg!(glutin) {
    // use glutin
} else {
    // Do something else
}
#[cfg(all(glutin, surfman))]
compile_error!("You cannot specify both `glutin` and `surfman` features");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#syntax-and-error-messages)Syntax and Error Messages

The aliase names are restricted to the same rules as rust identifiers which, for one, means that they cannot have dashes ( `-` ) in them. Additionally, if you get certain syntax elements wrong, such as the alias name, the macro will error saying that the recursion limit was reached instead of giving a clear indication of what actually went wrong. This is due to a nuance with the macro parser and it might be fixed in a later release of this crate. It is also possible that aliases with dashes in the name might be supported in a later release. Open an issue if that is something that you would like implemented.

Finally, you can also induce an infinite recursion by having rules that both reference each-other, but this isn’t a real limitation because that doesn’t make logical sense anyway:

[§](https://docs.rs#attribution-and-thanks)Attribution and Thanks

- Thanks to my God and Father who led me through figuring this out and to whome I owe everything.
- Thanks to @Yandros on the Rust forum for [showing me](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/3)some crazy macro hacks!
- Thanks to @sfackler for [pointing out](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/2)the way to make cargo add the cfg flags.
- Thanks to the authors of the `tectonic_cfg_support::target_cfg`[bringing it up](https://users.rust-lang.org/t/any-such-thing-as-cfg-aliases/40100/13)on the Rust forum.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_aliases.html)- aliases
- Create `cfg`aliases

# spidev - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/spidev/^0.7.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#spidev)Spidev

The `spidev` crate provides access to Linux spidev devices
from rust.  The wrapping of the interface is pretty direct
and shouldn’t cause any surprises.

Additional information on the interface may be found in
[the kernel documentation
for spidev](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/spi/spidev).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
extern crate spidev;
use std::io;
use std::io::prelude::*;
use spidev::{Spidev, SpidevOptions, SpidevTransfer, SpiModeFlags};
fn create_spi() -> io::Result<Spidev> {
    let mut spi = Spidev::open("/dev/spidev0.0")?;
    let options = SpidevOptions::new()
         .bits_per_word(8)
         .max_speed_hz(20_000)
         .mode(SpiModeFlags::SPI_MODE_0)
         .build();
    spi.configure(&options)?;
    Ok(spi)
}
/// perform half duplex operations using Read and Write traits
fn half_duplex(spi: &mut Spidev) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut rx_buf = [0_u8; 10];
    spi.write(&[0x01, 0x02, 0x03])?;
    spi.read(&mut rx_buf)?;
    println!("{:?}", rx_buf);
    Ok(())
}
/// Perform full duplex operations using Ioctl
fn full_duplex(spi: &mut Spidev) -> io::Result<()> {
    // "write" transfers are also reads at the same time with
    // the read having the same length as the write
    let tx_buf = [0x01, 0x02, 0x03];
    let mut rx_buf = [0; 3];
    {
        let mut transfer = SpidevTransfer::read_write(&tx_buf, &mut rx_buf);
        spi.transfer(&mut transfer)?;
    }
    println!("{:?}", rx_buf);
    Ok(())
}
fn main() {
    let mut spi = create_spi().unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", half_duplex(&mut spi).unwrap());
    println!("{:?}", full_duplex(&mut spi).unwrap());
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::spidevioctl::`- [SpidevTransfer](https://docs.rs/spidevioctl/type.SpidevTransfer.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Spidev](https://docs.rs/struct.Spidev.html)
- Provide high-level access to Linux Spidev Driver

Here you need to initialize everything your task will need for the duration of its lifetime.
The config allows you to access the configuration of the task.

Start is called between the creation of the task and the first call to pre/process.

Process is the most critical execution of the task.
The goal will be to produce the output message as soon as possible.
Use preprocess to prepare the task to make this method as short as possible.

[Source](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/cu29_runtime/cutask.rs.html#459-461)[§](https://docs.rs#method.debug_state_type_path)#### fn [debug_state_type_path](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSrcTask.html#method.debug_state_type_path)() -> &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/cu29_runtime/cutask.rs.html#459-461)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.debug_state_type_path)

#### fn [debug_state_type_path](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSrcTask.html#method.debug_state_type_path)() -> &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Returns the reflected type path used as this task’s debug-state schema.

This is a method called by the runtime before “process”. This is a kind of best effort,
as soon as possible call to give a chance for the task to do some work before to prepare
to make “process” as short as possible.

This is a method called by the runtime after “process”. It is best effort a chance for
the task to update some state after process is out of the way.
It can be use for example to maintain statistics etc. that are not time-critical for the robot.

# arrow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrow/^58.3/

## Expand description

A complete, safe, native Rust implementation of [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org), a cross-language
development platform for in-memory data.

Please see the [arrow crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/arrow)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#columnar-format)Columnar Format

The [ array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) module provides statically typed implementations of all the array types as defined
by the

[Arrow Columnar Format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html)

For example, an [ Int32Array](https://docs.rs/array/type.Int32Array.html) represents a nullable array of

`i32````
let array = Int32Array::from(vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.len(), 3);
assert_eq!(array.value(0), 1);
assert_eq!(array.is_null(1), true);
let collected: Vec<_> = array.iter().collect();
assert_eq!(collected, vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.values(), &[1, 0, 3])
```
It is also possible to write generic code for different concrete types. For example, since the following function is generic over all primitively typed arrays, when invoked the Rust compiler will generate specialized implementations with optimized code for each concrete type.

```
fn sum<T: ArrowPrimitiveType>(array: &PrimitiveArray<T>) -> T::Native
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: Sum
{
    array.iter().map(|v| v.unwrap_or_default()).sum()
}
assert_eq!(sum(&Float32Array::from(vec![1.1, 2.9, 3.])), 7.);
assert_eq!(sum(&TimestampNanosecondArray::from(vec![1, 2, 3])), 6);
```
And the following uses [ ArrayAccessor](https://docs.rs/array/trait.ArrayAccessor.html) to implement a generic function
over all arrays with comparable values.

```
fn min<T: ArrayAccessor>(array: T) -> Option<T::Item>
where
    T::Item: Ord
{
    ArrayIter::new(array).filter_map(|v| v).min()
}
assert_eq!(min(&Int32Array::from(vec![4, 2, 1, 6])), Some(1));
assert_eq!(min(&StringArray::from(vec!["b", "a", "c"])), Some("a"));
```
**For more examples, and details consult the  arrow_array docs.**

[§](https://docs.rs#type-erasure--trait-objects)Type Erasure / Trait Objects

It is common to write code that handles any type of array, without necessarily
knowing its concrete type. This is done using the [ Array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) trait and using

[to determine the appropriate](https://docs.rs/datatypes/enum.DataType.html)

`DataType``downcast_ref`.```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `StringArray`
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `Float32Array`
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
You can use the [ AsArray](https://docs.rs/array/trait.AsArray.html) extension trait to facilitate downcasting:

```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_string()),
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_primitive()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
It is also common to want to write a function that returns one of a number of possible
array implementations. [ ArrayRef](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html) is a type-alias for

[which is frequently used for this purpose](https://docs.rs/array/trait.Array.html)

`Arc<dyn Array>````
fn parse_to_primitive<'a, T, I>(iter: I) -> PrimitiveArray<T>
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: FromStr,
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    PrimitiveArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(|val| T::Native::from_str(val).ok()))
}
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: DataType) -> ArrayRef
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
   match to_data_type {
       DataType::Int32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<Int32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       DataType::UInt32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<UInt32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       _ => unimplemented!()
   }
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], DataType::Int32);
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<Int32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compute-kernels)Compute Kernels

The [ compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html) module provides optimised implementations of many common operations,
for example the

`parse_strings` operation above could also be implemented as follows:```
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: &DataType) -> Result<ArrayRef>
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    let array = StringArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(Some));
    arrow::compute::cast(&array, to_data_type)
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], &DataType::UInt32).unwrap();
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<UInt32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
This module also implements many common vertical operations:

- All mathematical binary operators, such as `sub`
- All boolean binary operators such as `equality`
- `cast`
- `filter`
- `take`
- `sort`
- some string operators such as `substring``length`

```
let array = Int32Array::from_iter(0..100);
// Create a 32-bit integer scalar (single) value:
let scalar = Int32Array::new_scalar(60);
// find all rows in the array that are greater than 60
let predicate = gt(&array, &scalar).unwrap();
// copy all matching rows into a new array
let filtered = filter(&array, &predicate).unwrap();
let expected = Int32Array::from_iter(61..100);
assert_eq!(&expected, filtered.as_primitive::<Int32Type>());
```
As well as some horizontal operations, such as:

[§](https://docs.rs#tabular-representation)Tabular Representation

It is common to want to group one or more columns together into a tabular representation. This
is provided by [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) which combines a

[and a corresponding list of](https://docs.rs/datatypes/struct.Schema.html)

`Schema`[.](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html)

`ArrayRef````
let col_1 = Arc::new(Int32Array::from_iter([1, 2, 3])) as _;
let col_2 = Arc::new(Float32Array::from_iter([1., 6.3, 4.])) as _;
let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter([("col1", col_1), ("col_2", col_2)]).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-printing)Pretty Printing

See the [ util::pretty](https://docs.rs/util/pretty/index.html) module (requires the

`prettyprint` crate feature)[§](https://docs.rs#io)IO

This crate provides readers and writers for various formats to/from `RecordBatch`

Support for [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) is published as a [separate parquet crate](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)

Support for [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org/) is published as a [separate arrow-avro crate](https://crates.io/crates/arrow-avro)

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-compatibility)Serde Compatibility

[ arrow_json::reader::Decoder](https://docs.rs/arrow-json/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_json/reader/struct.Decoder.html) provides a mechanism to convert arbitrary, serde-compatible
structures into

[.](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Whilst likely less performant than implementing a custom builder, as described in
[arrow_array::builder](https://docs.rs/array/builder/index.html), this provides a simple mechanism to get up and running quickly

```
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct MyStruct {
    int32: i32,
    string: String,
}
let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("int32", DataType::Int32, false),
    Field::new("string", DataType::Utf8, false),
]);
let rows = vec![
    MyStruct{ int32: 5, string: "bar".to_string() },
    MyStruct{ int32: 8, string: "foo".to_string() },
];
let mut decoder = ReaderBuilder::new(Arc::new(schema)).build_decoder().unwrap();
decoder.serialize(&rows).unwrap();
let batch = decoder.flush().unwrap().unwrap();
// Expect batch containing two columns
let int32 = batch.column(0).as_primitive::<Int32Type>();
assert_eq!(int32.values(), &[5, 8]);
let string = batch.column(1).as_string::<i32>();
assert_eq!(string.value(0), "bar");
assert_eq!(string.value(1), "foo");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-topology)Crate Topology

The [ arrow](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs) project is implemented as multiple sub-crates, which are then re-exported by
this top-level crate.

Crate authors can choose to depend on this top-level crate, or just the sub-crates they need.

The current list of sub-crates is:

- `arrow-arith`
- `arrow-array`
- `arrow-buffer`
- `arrow-cast`
- `arrow-csv`
- `arrow-data`
- `arrow-ipc`
- `arrow-json`
- `arrow-ord`
- `arrow-row`
- `arrow-schema`
- `arrow-select`
- `arrow-string`

Some functionality is also distributed independently of this crate:

- `arrow-flight`- [Arrow Flight RPC](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Flight.html)
- `parquet`- [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/)
- `arrow-avro`- [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org/)

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This project follows the [Apache Arrow Security Model](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/dev/format/Security.html).

Unexpected behavior (e.g., panics, crashes, or infinite loops) triggered by
malformed input is considered a **bug**, not a security vulnerability,
unless it is **exploitable** by an attacker to

- Execute arbitrary code (Remote Code Execution);
- Exfiltrate sensitive information from process memory (Information Disclosure);

If you think you have found a security vulnerability, please follow the
reporting instructions in the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Like many crates, this crate makes use of `unsafe` where prudent. However, it endeavors to be
sound. Specifically, **it should not be possible to trigger undefined behavior using safe APIs.**

Undefined behavior using safe APIs is considered a bug, not a security
vulnerability, unless it can be exploited. Please see the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for details.

For more information on the use of `unsafe`, see [here](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/tree/main/arrow#safety).

[§](https://docs.rs#higher-level-processing)Higher-level Processing

This crate aims to provide reusable, low-level primitives for operating on columnar data. For
more sophisticated query processing workloads, consider checking out [DataFusion](https://github.com/apache/arrow-datafusion). This
orchestrates the primitives exported by this crate into an embeddable query engine, with
SQL and DataFrame frontends, and heavily influences this crate’s roadmap.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# itertools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/itertools/^0.14.0/

## Expand description

Extra iterator adaptors, functions and macros.

To extend [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) with methods in this crate, import
the

[trait:](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html)

`Itertools``use itertools::Itertools;`Now, new methods like [ interleave](https://docs.rs/trait.Itertools.html#method.interleave)
are available on all iterators:

```
use itertools::Itertools;
let it = (1..3).interleave(vec![-1, -2]);
itertools::assert_equal(it, vec![1, -1, 2, -2]);
```
Most iterator methods are also provided as functions (with the benefit
that they convert parameters using [ IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)):

```
use itertools::interleave;
for elt in interleave(&[1, 2, 3], &[2, 3, 4]) {
    /* loop body */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

- `use_std`- Enabled by default.
- Disable to compile itertools using `#![no_std]`. This disables any item that depend on allocations (see the`use_alloc`feature) and hash maps (like`unique`,`counts`,`into_grouping_map`and more).

- `use_alloc`- Enabled by default.
- Enables any item that depend on allocations (like `chunk_by`,`kmerge`,`join`and many more).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of itertools requires Rust 1.63.0 or later.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::`- [structs](https://docs.rs/structs/index.html)::*;

# re_log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_log/=0.34.0-rc.4/

## Expand description

Text logging (nothing to do with rerun logging) for use in rerun libraries.

Provides helpers for adding multiple loggers, and for setting up logging on native and on web.

- `trace`: spammy things
- `debug`: things that might be useful when debugging
- `info`: things that we want to show to users
- `warn`: problems that we can recover from
- `error`: problems that lead to loss of functionality or data

The `warn_once` etc macros are for when you want to suppress repeated
logging of the exact same message.

In the viewer these logs, if >= info, become notifications. See
`re_ui::notifications` for more information.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [external](https://docs.rs/external/index.html)
- Re-exports of other crates.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [debug](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)
- Constructs an event at the debug level.

- Like `std::debug_assert!`

- Like `std::debug_assert_eq!`

- Panics in debug builds with a “DEBUG PANIC: “ prefix.

- Log a warning in debug builds, or a debug message in release builds.

- Like `debug_warn!`

# re_log_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_log_types/=0.34.0-rc.4/

## Expand description

The different types that make up the rerun log format.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

*No documented features in Cargo.toml*

[§](https://docs.rs#mono-components)Mono-components

Some components, mostly transform related ones, are “mono-components”. This means that Rerun makes assumptions that depend on this component only taking on a singular value for all instances of an Entity. Where possible, exposed APIs will force these components to be logged as a singular instance. However, it is an error with undefined behavior to manually use lower-level APIs to log a batched mono-component.

This requirement is especially apparent with transforms:
Each entity must have a unique transform chain,
e.g. the entity `foo/bar/baz` is has the transform that is the product of
`foo.transform * foo/bar.transform * foo/bar/baz.transform`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use self::arrow_msg::`- [ArrowMsg](https://docs.rs/arrow_msg/struct.ArrowMsg.html);
- `pub use self::arrow_msg::`- [ArrowRecordBatchReleaseCallback](https://docs.rs/arrow_msg/struct.ArrowRecordBatchReleaseCallback.html);
- `pub use self::`- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arrow_](https://docs.rs/arrow_msg/index.html)- msg
- `ArrowMsg`- `crate::LogMsg`
- [example_](https://docs.rs/example_components/index.html)- components
- Example components to be used for tests and docs
- [external](https://docs.rs/external/index.html)
- [hash](https://docs.rs/hash/index.html)
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)
- Every logged entity in Rerun is logged to an `EntityPath`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [entity_](https://docs.rs/macro.entity_path.html)- path
- Build an `EntityPath`*not*escaped:
- [entity_](https://docs.rs/macro.entity_path_vec.html)- path_ - vec
- Build a `Vec<EntityPathPart>`:
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_into_enum.html)- into_ - enum

- [Timeline](https://docs.rs/struct.TimelinePoint.html)- Point
- A point on a timeline
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html)
- Encodes a timestamp in nanoseconds since unix epoch.

# re_sdk_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_sdk_types/=0.34.0-rc.4/

## Expand description

The standard Rerun data types, component types, and archetypes.

This crate contains both the IDL definitions for Rerun types (flatbuffers) as well as the code
generated from those using `re_types_builder`.

All builtin archetypes, components, datatypes and view definitions can be found in their respective top-level modules.

[§](https://docs.rs#contributing)Contributing

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

- `definitions/`contains IDL definitions for all Rerun types (data, components, archetypes).
- `src/`contains the code generated for Rust.
- `rerun_py/rerun/rerun2/`(at the root of this workspace) contains the code generated for Python.

While most of the code in this crate is auto-generated, some manual extensions are littered
throughout: look for files ending in `_ext.rs`, `_ext.py`, or `_ext.cpp` (also see the “Extensions”
section of this document).

[§](https://docs.rs#build-cache)Build cache

Updating either the source code of the code generator itself (`re_types_builder`) or any of the
.fbs files should re-trigger the code generation process the next time `re_sdk_types` is built.
Manual extension files will be left untouched.

Caching is controlled by a versioning hash that is stored in `store_hash.txt`.
If you suspect something is wrong with the caching mechanism and that your changes aren’t taken
into account when they should, try and remove `source_hash.txt`.
If that fixes the issue, you’ve found a bug.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-add-a-new-datatypecomponentarchetype)How-to: add a new datatype/component/archetype

Create the appropriate .fbs file in the appropriate place, and make sure it gets included in
some way (most likely indirectly) by `archetypes.fbs`, which is the main entrypoint for
codegen.
Generally, the easiest thing to do is to add your new type to one of the centralized manifests,
e.g. for a new component, include it into `components.fbs`.

Your file should get picked up automatically by the code generator. Once the code for your new component has been generated, implement whatever extensions you need and make sure to tests any custom constructors you add.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-remove-an-existing-datatypecomponentarchetype)How-to: remove an existing datatype/component/archetype

Simply get rid of the type in question and rebuild `re_sdk_types` to trigger codegen.

Beware though: if you remove a whole definition file re-running codegen will not remove the associated generated files, you’ll have to do that yourself.

[§](https://docs.rs#extensions)Extensions

[§](https://docs.rs#rust)Rust

Generated Rust code can be manually extended by adding sibling files with the `_ext.rs`
prefix. E.g. to extend `vec2d.rs`, create a `vec2d_ext.rs`.

Trigger the codegen (e.g. by removing `source_hash.txt`) to generate the right `mod` clauses
automatically.

The simplest way to get started is to look at any of the existing examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#python)Python

Generated Python code can be manually extended by adding a sibling file with the `_ext.py`
prefix. E.g. to extend `vec2d.py`, create a `vec2d_ext.py`.

This sibling file needs to implement an extension class that is mixed in with the auto-generated class. The simplest way to get started is to look at any of the existing examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#c)C++

Generated C++ code can be manually extended by adding a sibling file with the `_ext.cpp` suffix.
E.g. to extend `vec2d.cpp`, create a `vec2d_ext.cpp`.

The sibling file is compiled as-is as part of the `rerun_cpp` crate.

Any include directive used in the extension is automatically added to the generated header, except to the generated header itself.

In order to extend the generated type declaration in the header,
you can specify a single code-block that you want to be injected into the type declaration by
starting it with `<CODEGEN_COPY_TO_HEADER>` and ending it with `</CODEGEN_COPY_TO_HEADER>`.
Note that it is your responsibility to make sure that the cpp file is valid C++ code -
the code generator & build will not adjust the extension file for you!

[§](https://docs.rs#language-specific-documentation)Language-specific documentation

You can prefix any doc comment line with `\{tag}`, where `{tag}` is one of `py`, `cpp`, `rs`,
and that part of the docs will only be present in the files generated for that specific
language.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

You can add an example to `docs/snippets/all`, and then include its source code in
the docs using the `\example` tag. The example will also be included in the list of
examples for type’s generated docs.

The `\example` tag supports the following arguments:

- `title`: a short description of the example which will be shown before the source code
- `image`: a link to an image, with special handling for images uploaded using- `scripts/upload_image.py`to- `static.rerun.io`
- `!api`: if present, the example will- *not*be included in comments embedded in the generated code

`\example example_file_name title="Some title" image="https://link.to/any_image.png"`If the url does not start with `https://static.rerun.io/`, then it will be used as the
`src` attribute in an `img` HTML tag, without any changes:

`<img src="https://link.to/any_image.png">`Otherwise the URL is treated as a rerun screenshot, which expects the following link format:

`https://static.rerun.io/{name}/{hash}/{max_width}.{ext}`These parameters will be used to generate an image stack:

- `name`: the original filename of the uploaded screenshot, without its extension
- `hash`: the content hash of the original screenshot
- `max_width`: the maximum width available for this screenshot.- If the value is not a valid integer suffixed by `w`(e.g.`1200w`), then the image stack will only include the`full`size.
- If the value *is*a valid integer, then sizes*larger*than the value will be omitted from the stack.

- If the value is not a valid integer suffixed by
- `ext`: the file extension of the image (- `png`,- `jpeg`, etc.)

Given a URL like `https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/1024w.png`,
the docs codegen will generate the following image stack:

```
<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 480px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/480w.png">
  <source media="(max-width: 768px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/768w.png">
  <source media="(max-width: 1024px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/1024w.png">
  <img src="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/full.png" alt="screenshot of {title} example">
</picture>
```
The `1200px` size was omitted from the stack.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-this-with-scriptsupload_imagepy)How to use this with `scripts/upload_image.py`

Running `scripts/upload_image.py {file}` will generate an image stack.
You need to take the *maximum width* available in that stack, and use it as the value of `image=` in `\example`.

For example, if the image stack generated by the script is:

```
<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 480px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/480w.png">
  <source media="(max-width: 768px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/768w.png">
  <source media="(max-width: 1024px)" srcset="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/1024w.png">
  <img src="https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/full.png">
</picture>
```
Then the url you should use is `https://static.rerun.io/my_screenshot/9066060e59ee9d2d7d98b214b8db0b8f2e8ab4b8/1024w.png`.

It works this way because `upload_image.py` does not upscale screenshots, it only downscales them.
We need to know what the maximum width we can use is, because we can’t just provide all the widths all the time.
If the currently-used `max-width` source fails to load, it will show the blank image icon.
There is no way to provide a fallback in `<picture>` if a specific `max-width` source fails to load.
Browsers will not automatically try to load the other sources!

- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_avc_chunk_to_nalu_stream.html)- avc_ - chunk_ - to_ - nalu_ - stream
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_hevc_chunk_to_annexb.html)- hevc_ - chunk_ - to_ - annexb
- Write an H.265 chunk to an Annex B stream without state tracking.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_hevc_chunk_to_nalu_stream.html)- hevc_ - chunk_ - to_ - nalu_ - stream

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2.0/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# re_mp4_reader - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/re_mp4_reader/0.34.0-rc.4/target-redirect/re_mp4_reader/

## Expand description

Core mp4-to-chunk loading logic for Rerun.

Reads any `.mp4` file (or its in-memory bytes) and emits an iterator of
[ re_chunk::Chunk](https://docs.rs/re_chunk/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_chunk/chunk/struct.Chunk.html)s ready to be sent to a recording or chunk store.

Two output modes are supported via [ Mode](https://docs.rs/enum.Mode.html):

- `Mode::Asset`- `re_sdk_types::archetypes::AssetVideo`- `re_sdk_types::archetypes::VideoFrameReference`
- `Mode::Stream`- `re_video`- `re_sdk_types::archetypes::VideoStream`- `VideoSample`/- `IsKeyframe`chunks.

The entry point is [ load_mp4_from_bytes](https://docs.rs/fn.load_mp4_from_bytes.html), with a native-only

`load_mp4`
convenience wrapper that reads the bytes from a path on disk.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Mp4Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html)
- Configuration for `crate::load_mp4_from_bytes`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Mode](https://docs.rs/enum.Mode.html)
- Output mode for `crate::load_mp4_from_bytes`
- [Mp4Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Mp4Error.html)
- Errors produced by the mp4 reader.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_mp4.html)- mp4
- Load an mp4 file from disk and return an iterator of chunks.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_mp4_from_bytes.html)- mp4_ - from_ - bytes
- Load mp4 bytes from memory and return an iterator of chunks.

---

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/re_mp4_reader/0.34.0-rc.4/src/re_mp4_reader/lib.rs.html

# re_mp4_reader/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Core mp4-to-chunk loading logic for Rerun.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Reads any `.mp4` file (or its in-memory bytes) and emits an iterator of
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`re_chunk::Chunk`]s ready to be sent to a recording or chunk store.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Two output modes are supported via [`Mode`]:
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! - [`Mode::Asset`] — emit an [`re_sdk_types::archetypes::AssetVideo`] blob
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!   chunk plus a [`re_sdk_types::archetypes::VideoFrameReference`] index chunk.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - [`Mode::Stream`] — demux the mp4 with [`re_video`] and emit a static
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   [`re_sdk_types::archetypes::VideoStream`] codec chunk followed by per-GOP
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!   (or per-sample) `VideoSample` / `IsKeyframe` chunks.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! The entry point is [`load_mp4_from_bytes`], with a native-only `load_mp4`
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! convenience wrapper that reads the bytes from a path on disk.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)mod asset;
[17](https://docs.rs#17)mod config;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)mod error;
[19](https://docs.rs#19)mod stream;
[20](https://docs.rs#20)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)pub use config::{Mode, Mp4Config};
[22](https://docs.rs#22)pub use error::Mp4Error;
[23](https://docs.rs#23)
[24](https://docs.rs#24)use itertools::Either;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)
[26](https://docs.rs#26)use re_chunk::{Chunk, EntityPath};
[27](https://docs.rs#27)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)/// Load an mp4 file from disk and return an iterator of chunks.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)///
[30](https://docs.rs#30)/// See [`Mp4Config`] for the available modes. The iterator may yield `Err`
[31](https://docs.rs#31)/// items for individual chunk failures; callers may skip them.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)///
[33](https://docs.rs#33)/// In [`Mode::Stream`], chunks are produced by streaming the file from disk —
[34](https://docs.rs#34)/// only the container metadata and one GOP's worth of sample bytes are resident
[35](https://docs.rs#35)/// at a time, so the whole video is never loaded into memory. [`Mode::Asset`]
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// still reads the whole file, since it logs the mp4 as a single blob.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]
[38](https://docs.rs#38)pub fn load_mp4(
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    path: &std::path::Path,
[40](https://docs.rs#40)    config: &Mp4Config,
[41](https://docs.rs#41)    entity_path: &EntityPath,
[42](https://docs.rs#42)) -> Result<impl Iterator<Item = Result<Chunk, Mp4Error>> + use<>, Mp4Error> {
[43](https://docs.rs#43)    re_tracing::profile_function!();
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    let debug_name = path.display().to_string();
[45](https://docs.rs#45)    match &config.mode {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)        Mode::Asset { timepoint } => Ok(Either::Left(new_asset_iter(
[47](https://docs.rs#47)            std::fs::read(path)?,
[48](https://docs.rs#48)            config,
[49](https://docs.rs#49)            entity_path,
[50](https://docs.rs#50)            timepoint.clone(),
[51](https://docs.rs#51)        )?)),
[52](https://docs.rs#52)
[53](https://docs.rs#53)        Mode::Stream {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)            chunk_by_gop,
[55](https://docs.rs#55)            allow_b_frames,
[56](https://docs.rs#56)        } => {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)            let file = std::fs::File::open(path)?;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)            let size = file.metadata()?.len();
[59](https://docs.rs#59)            let iter = stream::iter_chunks(
[60](https://docs.rs#60)                std::io::BufReader::new(file),
[61](https://docs.rs#61)                size,
[62](https://docs.rs#62)                entity_path,
[63](https://docs.rs#63)                &config.timeline_name,
[64](https://docs.rs#64)                *chunk_by_gop,
[65](https://docs.rs#65)                config.timeline_type,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)                *allow_b_frames,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)                &debug_name,
[68](https://docs.rs#68)            )?;
[69](https://docs.rs#69)            Ok(Either::Right(iter))
[70](https://docs.rs#70)        }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    }
[72](https://docs.rs#72)}
[73](https://docs.rs#73)
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// Load mp4 bytes from memory and return an iterator of chunks.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// The returned iterator is lazy: chunks are constructed one at a time as it is
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// drained. The item type is `Result<Chunk, Mp4Error>` because constructing an
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// individual chunk can fail mid-stream; it is up to the caller to decide
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// whether to abort or skip on `Err`. Note that *unreadable frame timestamps*
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// are not surfaced as an `Err` item — that case is handled leniently by
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// emitting only the asset chunk.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)///
[83](https://docs.rs#83)/// `debug_name` is a human-readable label for the video (e.g. its source path
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// or URL) used only in log and panic messages — it has no effect on decoding.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// Unlike the path-based [`load_mp4`], the bytes are already in memory here, so
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// [`Mode::Stream`] reads samples from the in-memory buffer rather than streaming
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// from disk.
[89](https://docs.rs#89)pub fn load_mp4_from_bytes(
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    bytes: Vec<u8>,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    config: &Mp4Config,
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    entity_path: &EntityPath,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    debug_name: &str,
[94](https://docs.rs#94)) -> Result<impl Iterator<Item = Result<Chunk, Mp4Error>> + use<>, Mp4Error> {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    re_tracing::profile_function!();
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    match &config.mode {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)        Mode::Asset { timepoint } => Ok(Either::Left(new_asset_iter(
[98](https://docs.rs#98)            bytes,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)            config,
[100](https://docs.rs#100)            entity_path,
[101](https://docs.rs#101)            timepoint.clone(),
[102](https://docs.rs#102)        )?)),
[103](https://docs.rs#103)
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        Mode::Stream {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)            chunk_by_gop,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)            allow_b_frames,
[107](https://docs.rs#107)        } => {
[108](https://docs.rs#108)            let size = bytes.len() as u64;
[109](https://docs.rs#109)            let iter = stream::iter_chunks(
[110](https://docs.rs#110)                std::io::Cursor::new(bytes),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)                size,
[112](https://docs.rs#112)                entity_path,
[113](https://docs.rs#113)                &config.timeline_name,
[114](https://docs.rs#114)                *chunk_by_gop,
[115](https://docs.rs#115)                config.timeline_type,
[116](https://docs.rs#116)                *allow_b_frames,
[117](https://docs.rs#117)                debug_name,
[118](https://docs.rs#118)            )?;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)            Ok(Either::Right(iter))
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    }
[122](https://docs.rs#122)}
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)fn new_asset_iter(
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    bytes: Vec<u8>,
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    config: &Mp4Config,
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    entity_path: &EntityPath,
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    timepoint: re_chunk::TimePoint,
[129](https://docs.rs#129)) -> Result<asset::AssetChunkIter, Mp4Error> {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    asset::AssetChunkIter::new(
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        bytes,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        entity_path,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        config.timeline_name,
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        config.timeline_type,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        timepoint,
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    )
[137](https://docs.rs#137)}

# Mode in re_mp4_reader - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_mp4_reader/0.34.0-rc.4/re_mp4_reader/enum.Mode.html

```
pub enum Mode {
    Asset {
        timepoint:
```
[TimePoint](https://docs.rs/re_log_types/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_log_types/index/time_point/struct.TimePoint.html),
    },
    Stream {
        chunk_by_gop: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
        allow_b_frames: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
    },
}## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Asset)

### Asset

Emit an `AssetVideo` blob chunk plus a `VideoFrameReference` index chunk.

`timepoint` is placed on the `AssetVideo` blob chunk. Public callers
generally pass `TimePoint::default()` (static); the file importer passes
its enriched timepoint with a zero-duration cell on the `video`
timeline plus any `created_at` / `modified_at` cells.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Stream)

### Stream

Emit a static `VideoStream(codec=…)` chunk followed by per-sample
`VideoSample` chunks at PTS.

The timeline used for the samples is named [ Mp4Config::timeline_name](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html#structfield.timeline_name)
and typed

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html#structfield.timeline_type)

`Mp4Config::timeline_type`#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Stream.field.chunk_by_gop)

`chunk_by_gop: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)Should the sampls be grouped into one Rerun chunk per GOP?

If `true`, groups samples into one Rerun chunk per GOP (keyframe through the sample just
before the next keyframe). Otherwise, emits one Rerun chunk per sample.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Stream.field.allow_b_frames)

`allow_b_frames: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)Opts in to mp4s with B-frames, which the `VideoStream` archetype does not yet model
(DTS != PTS — see issue #10090).

When `true`, the emitted time column is marked unsorted because PTS values in decode
order may not be monotonic. Intended to be combined with a downstream transcode step
that drops the B-frames.

# re_video - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_video/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_video/index.html

## Expand description

Video decoding library.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use re_mp4::`- [TrackId](https://docs.rs/re_mp4/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_mp4/types/type.TrackId.html);
- `pub use re_mp4::`- [TrackKind](https://docs.rs/re_mp4/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_mp4/types/enum.TrackKind.html);
- `pub use re_quota_channel::`- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/re_quota_channel/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_quota_channel/sync/struct.Receiver.html);
- `pub use re_quota_channel::`- [Sender](https://docs.rs/re_quota_channel/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_quota_channel/sync/struct.Sender.html);
- `pub use re_quota_channel::`- [TryRecvError](https://docs.rs/crossbeam-channel/0.5.15/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/crossbeam_channel/err/enum.TryRecvError.html);
- `pub use re_span::`- [Span](https://docs.rs/re_span/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_span/struct.Span.html);
- `pub use stable_index_deque::StableIndexDeque;`
- `pub use time::Time;`
- `pub use time::Timescale;`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [player](https://docs.rs/player/index.html)
- Video player for decoding video frames over time.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AnnexB](https://docs.rs/struct.AnnexBStreamState.html)- Stream - State
- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/struct.Chunk.html)
- One chunk of encoded video data, representing a single `crate::SampleMetadata`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodeSettings.html)- Settings
- Settings for video decoding.
- [Decoded](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodedFrameContent.html)- Frame - Content
- CPU-side data for a decoded frame.
- [FFmpeg](https://docs.rs/struct.FFmpegVersion.html)- Version
- A successfully parsed `FFmpeg`version.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html)
- One decoded video frame.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameInfo.html)- Info
- Meta information about a decoded video frame, as reported by the decoder.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/struct.SampleMetadata.html)- Metadata
- [Samples](https://docs.rs/struct.SamplesStatistics.html)- Statistics
- Meta information about the video samples.
- [Video](https://docs.rs/struct.VideoDataDescription.html)- Data - Description
- Description of video data.
- [Video](https://docs.rs/struct.VideoEncodingDetails.html)- Encoding - Details
- Various information about how the video was encoded.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Chroma](https://docs.rs/enum.ChromaSubsamplingModes.html)- Subsampling - Modes
- Chroma subsampling mode.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeHardwareAcceleration.html)- Hardware - Acceleration

- Result of a successful GOP detection.

- Pixel format/layout used by `FrameContent::data`

- The state of the current sample.
- [Video](https://docs.rs/enum.VideoCodec.html)- Codec
- The basic codec family used to encode the video.
- [Video](https://docs.rs/enum.VideoDeliveryMethod.html)- Delivery - Method
- Distinguishes static videos from potentially ongoing video streams.

- Errors that can occur when loading a video.

- [AV1_](https://docs.rs/constant.AV1_TEST_KEYFRAME.html)- TEST_ - KEYFRAME

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [channel](https://docs.rs/fn.channel.html)
- Create a channel for use with `new_decoder`
- [detect_](https://docs.rs/fn.detect_gop_start.html)- gop_ - start
- Try to determine whether a frame chunk is the start of a GOP.
- [enabled_](https://docs.rs/fn.enabled_features.html)- features
- [ffmpeg_](https://docs.rs/fn.ffmpeg_download_url.html)- download_ - url
- Download URL for the latest version of `FFmpeg`on the current platform. None if the platform is not supported.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_start_of_gop.html)- start_ - of_ - gop
- Is the given sample the start of a GOP (i.e. a keyframe/sync).
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_decoder.html)- decoder
- Creates a new async decoder for the given `video`data.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_avc_chunk_to_annexb.html)- avc_ - chunk_ - to_ - annexb
- Write an H.264 chunk to an Annex B stream without state tracking.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_avc_chunk_to_nalu_stream.html)- avc_ - chunk_ - to_ - nalu_ - stream
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_hevc_chunk_to_annexb.html)- hevc_ - chunk_ - to_ - annexb
- Write an H.265 chunk to an Annex B stream without state tracking.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_hevc_chunk_to_nalu_stream.html)- hevc_ - chunk_ - to_ - nalu_ - stream

# load_mp4_from_bytes in re_mp4_reader - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_mp4_reader/0.34.0-rc.4/re_mp4_reader/fn.load_mp4_from_bytes.html

```
pub fn load_mp4_from_bytes(
    bytes:
```
[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>,
    config: &[Mp4Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html),
    entity_path: &[EntityPath](https://docs.rs/re_log_types/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_log_types/path/entity_path/struct.EntityPath.html),
    debug_name: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<impl [Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)<Item = [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Chunk](https://docs.rs/re_chunk/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_chunk/chunk/struct.Chunk.html), [Mp4Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Mp4Error.html)>> + use<>, [Mp4Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Mp4Error.html)>## Expand description

Load mp4 bytes from memory and return an iterator of chunks.

The returned iterator is lazy: chunks are constructed one at a time as it is
drained. The item type is `Result<Chunk, Mp4Error>` because constructing an
individual chunk can fail mid-stream; it is up to the caller to decide
whether to abort or skip on `Err`. Note that *unreadable frame timestamps*
are not surfaced as an `Err` item — that case is handled leniently by
emitting only the asset chunk.

`debug_name` is a human-readable label for the video (e.g. its source path
or URL) used only in log and panic messages — it has no effect on decoding.

Unlike the path-based [ load_mp4](https://docs.rs/fn.load_mp4.html), the bytes are already in memory here, so

[reads samples from the in-memory buffer rather than streaming from disk.](https://docs.rs/enum.Mode.html#variant.Stream)

`Mode::Stream`

---

# load_mp4 in re_mp4_reader - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_mp4_reader/0.34.0-rc.4/re_mp4_reader/fn.load_mp4.html

```
pub fn load_mp4(
    path: &
```
[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html),
    config: &[Mp4Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html),
    entity_path: &[EntityPath](https://docs.rs/re_log_types/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_log_types/path/entity_path/struct.EntityPath.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<impl [Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)<Item = [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Chunk](https://docs.rs/re_chunk/0.34.0-rc.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/re_chunk/chunk/struct.Chunk.html), [Mp4Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Mp4Error.html)>> + use<>, [Mp4Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Mp4Error.html)>## Expand description

Load an mp4 file from disk and return an iterator of chunks.

See [ Mp4Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Mp4Config.html) for the available modes. The iterator may yield

`Err`
items for individual chunk failures; callers may skip them.In [ Mode::Stream](https://docs.rs/enum.Mode.html#variant.Stream), chunks are produced by streaming the file from disk —
only the container metadata and one GOP’s worth of sample bytes are resident
at a time, so the whole video is never loaded into memory.

[still reads the whole file, since it logs the mp4 as a single blob.](https://docs.rs/enum.Mode.html#variant.Asset)

`Mode::Asset`

# cu-lewansoul 1.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cu-lewansoul/1.0.0

## Lewansoul Serial Bus driver for Copper

This enables the communication with the Lewansoul bus servos as a Sink task on Copper.

`Lewansoul` can consume an owned serial resource via
`resources: { serial: \"<bundle>.serial3\" }` from
`cu_linux_resources::LinuxResources`.

See the crate [cu29](https://crates.io/crates/cu29) for more information about the Copper project.

---

[51](#51)fn compute_checksum(data: impl Iterator<Item = u8>) -> u8 {
[52](#52)    let mut checksum: u8 = 0;
[53](#53)    for byte in data {
[54](#54)        checksum = checksum.wrapping_add(byte);
[55](#55)    }
[56](#56)    !checksum

[89](#89)    fn from_bindings(
[90](#90)        manager: &'r mut ResourceManager,
[91](#91)        mapping: Option<&ResourceBindingMap<Self::Binding>>,
[92](#92)    ) -> CuResult<Self> {
[93](#93)        let mapping = mapping.ok_or_else(|| {
[94](#94)            CuError::from("Lewansoul requires a `serial` resource mapping in copperconfig")
[95](#95)        })?;
[96](#96)        let path = mapping.get(Binding::Serial).ok_or_else(|| {
[97](#97)            CuError::from("Lewansoul resources must include `serial: <bundle.resource>`")
[98](#98)        })?;
[99](#99)        let serial = manager
[100](#100)            .take::<LinuxSerialPort>(path.typed())
[101](#101)            .map_err(|e| e.add_cause("Failed to fetch Lewansoul serial resource"))?;
[102](#102)        Ok(Self { serial })
[103](#103)    }

[106](#106)impl Lewansoul {
[107](#107)    fn send_packet(&mut self, id: u8, command: u8, data: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
[108](#108)        let mut packet = vec![0x55, 0x55, id, data.len() as u8 + 3, command];
[109](#109)        packet.extend_from_slice(data);
[110](#110)        let checksum = compute_checksum(packet[2..].iter().copied());
[111](#111)        packet.push(checksum);
[112](#112)
[113](#113)        self.port.write_all(&packet)?;
[115](#115)        Ok(())
[116](#116)    }
[117](#117)
[118](#118)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[121](#121)    fn reassign_servo_id(&mut self, id: u8, new_id: u8) -> io::Result<()> {
[122](#122)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_ID_WRITE, &[new_id])?;
[123](#123)        self.read_response()?;
[124](#124)        Ok(())
[125](#125)    }
[126](#126)
[127](#127)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[128](#128)    fn read_current_position(&mut self, id: u8) -> io::Result<f32> {
[129](#129)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_POS_READ, &[])?;
[130](#130)        let response = self.read_response()?;
[131](#131)        Ok((i16::from_le_bytes([response.2[0], response.2[1]])) as f32 * 240.0 / 1000.0)
[132](#132)    }
[133](#133)
[134](#134)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[135](#135)    fn read_present_voltage(&mut self, id: u8) -> io::Result<f32> {
[136](#136)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_VIN_READ, &[])?;
[137](#137)        let response = self.read_response()?;
[138](#138)        Ok(u16::from_le_bytes([response.2[0], response.2[1]]) as f32 / 1000.0)
[139](#139)    }
[140](#140)
[141](#141)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[142](#142)    fn read_temperature(&mut self, id: u8) -> io::Result<u8> {
[143](#143)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_TEMP_READ, &[])?;
[144](#144)        let response = self.read_response()?;
[145](#145)        Ok(response.2[0])
[146](#146)    }
[147](#147)
[148](#148)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[149](#149)    fn read_angle_limits(&mut self, id: u8) -> io::Result<(f32, f32)> {
[150](#150)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_ANGLE_LIMIT_READ, &[])?;
[151](#151)        let response = self.read_response()?;
[152](#152)        Ok((
[153](#153)            (i16::from_le_bytes([response.2[0], response.2[1]]) as f32) * 240.0 / 1000.0,
[154](#154)            (i16::from_le_bytes([response.2[2], response.2[3]]) as f32) * 240.0 / 1000.0,
[155](#155)        ))
[156](#156)    }
[157](#157)
[158](#158)    #[allow(dead_code)]
[159](#159)    fn ping(&mut self, id: u8) -> CuResult<()> {
[160](#160)        self.send_packet(id, servo::SERVO_ID_READ, &[])
[161](#161)            .map_err(|e| CuError::new_with_cause("IO Error trying to write to the SBUS", e))?;
[162](#162)        let response = self.read_response().map_err(|e| {
[163](#163)            CuError::new_with_cause("IO Error trying to read the ping response from SBUS", e)
[164](#164)        })?;
[165](#165)
[166](#166)        if response.2[0] == id {
[167](#167)            Ok(())
[168](#168)        } else {
[169](#169)            Err(format!(
[170](#170)                "The servo ID {} did not respond to ping got {} as ID instead.",
[171](#171)                id, response.2[0]
[172](#172)            )
[173](#173)            .into())
[174](#174)        }
[175](#175)    }
[176](#176)
[177](#177)    fn read_response(&mut self) -> io::Result<(u8, u8, Vec<u8>)> {
[178](#178)        let mut header = [0; 5];
[179](#179)        self.port.read_exact(&mut header)?;
[180](#180)        if header[0] != 0x55 || header[1] != 0x55 {
[181](#181)            return Err(io::Error::other("Invalid header"));
[182](#182)        }
[183](#183)        let id = header[2];
[184](#184)        let length = header[3];
[185](#185)        let command = header[4];
[186](#186)        let mut remaining = vec![0; length as usize - 2]; self.port.read_exact(&mut remaining)?;
[188](#188)        let checksum = compute_checksum(
[189](#189)            header[2..]
[190](#190)                .iter()
[191](#191)                .chain(remaining[..remaining.len() - 1].iter())
[192](#192)                .copied(),
[193](#193)        );
[194](#194)        if checksum != *remaining.last().unwrap() {
[195](#195)            return Err(io::Error::other("Invalid checksum"));
[196](#196)        }
[197](#197)        Ok((id, command, remaining[..remaining.len() - 1].to_vec()))
[198](#198)    }
[199](#199)}

[214](#214)    fn new(config: Option<&ComponentConfig>, resources: Self::Resources<'_>) -> CuResult<Self>
[215](#215)    where
[216](#216)        Self: Sized,
[217](#217)    {
[218](#218)        let ComponentConfig(kv) =
[219](#219)            config.ok_or("RPGpio needs a config, None was passed as ComponentConfig")?;
[220](#220)
[221](#221)        let mut ids = [0u8; 8];
[222](#222)        for (i, id) in ids.iter_mut().enumerate() {
[223](#223)            match kv.get(format!("servo{i}").as_str()) {
[224](#224)                Some(servo) => *id = servo.clone().into(),
[225](#225)                None if i == 0 => {
[226](#226)                    return Err(
[227](#227)                        "You need to specify at least one servo ID to address (as \"servo0\")"
[228](#228)                            .into(),
[229](#229)                    );
[230](#230)                }
[231](#231)                None => break,
[232](#232)            }
[233](#233)        }
[234](#234)
[235](#235)        let port = resources.serial.0;
[236](#236)
[237](#237)        Ok(Lewansoul { port, ids })
[238](#238)    }

#### fn [new](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSinkTask.html#tymethod.new)(
    config: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[ComponentConfig](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/config/struct.ComponentConfig.html)>,
    resources: Self::[Resources](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSinkTask.html#associatedtype.Resources)<'_>,
) -> [CuResult](https://docs.rs/cu29-traits/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_traits/type.CuResult.html)<Self>

Here you need to initialize everything your task will need for the duration of its lifetime.
The config allows you to access the configuration of the task.

Process is the most critical execution of the task.
The goal will be to produce the output message as soon as possible.
Use preprocess to prepare the task to make this method as short as possible.

[Source](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/cu29_runtime/cutask.rs.html#611-613)[§](https://docs.rs#method.debug_state_type_path)#### fn [debug_state_type_path](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSinkTask.html#method.debug_state_type_path)() -> &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/cu29_runtime/cutask.rs.html#611-613)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.debug_state_type_path)

#### fn [debug_state_type_path](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cutask/trait.CuSinkTask.html#method.debug_state_type_path)() -> &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Returns the reflected type path used as this task’s debug-state schema.

Start is called between the creation of the task and the first call to pre/process.

This is a method called by the runtime before “process”. This is a kind of best effort,
as soon as possible call to give a chance for the task to do some work before to prepare
to make “process” as short as possible.

This is a method called by the runtime after “process”. It is best effort a chance for
the task to update some state after process is out of the way.
It can be use for example to maintain statistics etc. that are not time-critical for the robot.

This method is called by the framework when it wants to save the task state.
The default implementation is to encode nothing (stateless).
If you have a state, you need to implement this method.
